title: Tajziya: a parser federation for the classical languages of the human corpus, organised by family
description: Tajziya is a federation of parsers for the classical languages of the human written corpus, organised by genealogical family and built on the dhancha spine. Its registry holds 79 language and stage nodes taken from the author's candidate language matrix, each keyed by stage, script and corpus and carrying the matrix's own status, with every conflict in that source recorded rather than resolved. Parsing proceeds through the Project ILM layers (phonology, script pivot, orthography, segmentation, morphology, syntax) with CoNLL-U as the common output. One node parses: a Classical Sanskrit vowel-sandhi segmenter, in Python and JavaScript kept behaviour-identical by test, which returns every admissible segmentation. Every other node is bound to its family's frame, which refuses by name and points to the package that would build it. Shared engines are derived from the data by phenomenon, separating script mechanisms, which recur across unrelated lineages, from language mechanisms. The matrix's elimination rule computes each node's status from recorded corpus coverage, treats translation as lossy rather than as recovery, and declines to certify a minimum while the corpus universe and loss function remain open. Beyond the posters, every language and script the Project ILM registry lists (7,867 ISO 639-3 languages and 226 ISO 15924 scripts, the data its 3D explorer draws) is carried as a coverage node or a script frame that refuses by name, and each can be generated as a package. Every language is a module: a folder with a manifest, sources with their licences, attested examples and a port, judged by one generic acceptance test in isolation and in integration, and generated for each remaining language as a package ready to hand to a person or a model. The process work of building a language, a script module or a shared engine, choosing a source and recording coverage is written as AAB paintings, and every package carries its own painting and a hash-chained configuration record of the intent, prompts, responses, decisions and artifact versions of the work. The Sanskrit sutra text is taken from an MIT-licensed edition of all 3,983 sutras; a compilation whose terms restrict reposting is read only from a pinned local copy. The Sanskrit parser holds all 3,983 sutras with type, term and padaccheda, derived from ashtadhyayi.com's data (credited) and cross-checked against vidyut-prakriya (MIT), with a generated source review.
